title: Being a Good Digital Citizen
tagline: Respect, safety and wellbeing in online spaces.
description: The internet is a shared space, like a market or a community hall. This course is about how we treat each other there: being respectful, dealing with bullying and harassment, protecting children, and keeping a healthy balance between screens and the rest of life.
outcomes: Ask before sharing other people's photos
Refuse to spread hate and tribalism
Block, report and get help with bullying and harassment
Balance screen time and manage your digital footprint

modules.title: Respect online
modules.summary: Kind words, consent and refusing hate.

lessons.title: The same values online and offline
lessons.body:
Online, people cannot see your face or hear your tone of voice. Words can feel colder and hurt more than you meant. But the people reading are just as real as the people you meet at the market.

## A simple test
Before you post or reply, ask: **would I say this to the person's face, in front of my family?** If not, do not post it.

## Respectful habits
- Greet people and use their names.
- Disagree with **ideas**, not with the person. *"I see it differently, because..."* works better than insults.
- Do not write in capital letters. It reads as shouting.
- If you are angry, wait before replying. A message cannot be unsent once it has been read.
- Admit mistakes and apologise when you get something wrong.

## Your rights come with responsibilities
You have the right to express yourself and to privacy online, just as offline. Other people have the same rights. Insulting, threatening or spreading lies about someone can hurt them, and in some cases can break the law.

## Being a positive voice
You can make online spaces better:

- thank people who share useful information,
- welcome new members to groups,
- correct false information kindly,
- stand up for someone being picked on.

Small actions by many people decide whether a group is a good place to be.
key_points: Would you say it to their face?
Disagree with ideas, not people
Wait before replying when you are angry
lessons.try_it: Next time you disagree in a group, use: 'I see it differently, because...'

lessons.title: Asking before you share
lessons.body:
Photos and videos of other people belong partly to them. Sharing them without asking can embarrass, hurt or even endanger someone.

## Ask first
Before you post a photo with other people in it, ask: *"Is it okay if I put this on Facebook?"* Some people have good reasons not to want their picture online, like a difficult family situation or a job.

## Children
Be especially careful with photos of children, including your own:

- Do not show their school uniform, school name or home in public posts.
- Do not share photos of children in the bath or partly dressed, even if they look innocent. Once online, a picture can be copied and misused.
- Ask other parents before sharing photos of their children.

## Private messages stay private
Do not screenshot and forward someone's private messages to others without their permission. It breaks trust.

## Never share intimate images
Sharing intimate photos of someone without their consent is deeply harmful and can be a crime. If someone sends you such an image of another person, do not forward it. Delete it.

## People in difficult moments
Do not film and share people in accidents, fights, hospital or at funerals. They cannot agree, and their families may see it.

## If someone shares your photo
Ask them politely to remove it. If they refuse, use the app's **Report** button. Most platforms remove private images shared without consent.
key_points: Ask before posting photos of other people
Protect children's privacy in photos
Never forward intimate images of anyone
lessons.try_it: Look at your last few posts. Did everyone in your photos agree to be shared?

lessons.title: Refusing to spread hate
lessons.body:
**Hate speech** attacks people because of who they are: their tribe, region, religion, colour, sex, disability or political side. It spreads easily online and can lead to real violence.

## What it can look like
- Jokes and memes that mock a tribe or region.
- Messages blaming a whole group for a problem.
- Calling people animals or insulting names.
- Calls to exclude, beat or harm people.

Zambia's motto is **One Zambia, One Nation**. Online hate works against that, setting neighbours against each other.

## Why we share it
It often arrives as a "joke" from a friend, or during heated times like elections. People forward it without thinking about who it hurts.

## What you can do
- **Do not forward it**, even to criticise it. Forwarding helps it spread.
- **Say something** if you feel safe to: *"Let's not talk about people like that in this group."*
- **Report it** to the platform. Facebook and WhatsApp let you report messages and accounts.
- If it includes **threats of violence**, report it to the police.

## Criticism is not hate
You can criticise leaders, parties, decisions and ideas. That is part of democracy. Talk about what people **do**, not what group they belong to.

## Think about the person reading
Somewhere, a person from that tribe, region or faith reads the message. Would you want your children to read the same about you?
key_points: Hate speech attacks people for who they are
Do not forward it, even to criticise it
Criticise actions and ideas, not groups
lessons.try_it: If you see a tribal 'joke' this week, do not forward it.

modules.title: Bullying and harassment
modules.summary: Recognising it, blocking and reporting, and getting help.

lessons.title: Recognising online bullying
lessons.body:
**Online bullying** (cyberbullying) is when someone uses phones or the internet to hurt, frighten or embarrass another person again and again. It can happen to children and adults.

## What it can look like
- Repeated insulting or threatening messages.
- Spreading rumours or lies about someone.
- Sharing embarrassing photos or private messages.
- Making a fake account to pretend to be someone.
- Leaving someone out of a group on purpose and mocking them.
- Sending messages late at night to frighten someone.

## Why it hurts so much
Online bullying can follow a person everywhere, at any time, through their phone. Many people may see it. It can lead to fear, sadness, missing school or work, and in serious cases harm to the person's health.

## Signs someone may be bullied
- They seem upset or afraid after using their phone.
- They stop using their phone suddenly, or hide it.
- They avoid school, work, church or friends.

## If it is happening to you
- **It is not your fault.**
- **Do not reply** to the bully. Replies often make it worse.
- **Save the evidence**: take screenshots with the date and the sender's name or number.
- **Tell someone you trust.**

The next lesson shows exactly how to block and report.

## If you see it happening
Do not join in, laugh or forward it. Check on the person privately: *"I saw what they posted. Are you okay?"* That can mean a lot.
key_points: Bullying is repeated, hurtful behaviour
Do not reply; save screenshots
Check on people who are being bullied
lessons.try_it: Think of one trusted person you would tell if you were bullied online.

lessons.title: How to block and report
lessons.body:
Every major app lets you **block** people so they cannot contact you, and **report** them to the company.

## WhatsApp
1. Open the chat with the person.
2. Tap their name at the top.
3. Scroll down and tap **Block**. You can also tap **Report**, which sends the last few messages to WhatsApp.

Blocked people cannot call or message you, or see your updates. They are not told they were blocked.

To block someone from adding you to groups, go to **Settings, Privacy, Groups** and choose **My contacts**.

## Facebook
- **On a profile:** tap the three dots, then **Block** or **Find support or report**.
- **On a post or comment:** tap the three dots, then **Report**, and choose the reason, such as harassment or hate speech.

You can also **restrict** or **unfriend** someone, or set your posts to Friends only.

## Calls and SMS
On most Android phones, open the phone app, press and hold the number in your call list, and tap **Block**.

## Before you block
**Save evidence first**. Take screenshots of the messages with the number or name visible. If you need to go to the police later, you will need them.

## When to go further
If messages include **threats of violence**, demands for money, or sharing intimate images, go to the **police** with your screenshots. These are serious matters, and the police take reports of online crime.
key_points: Screenshot the evidence first
Block and report in WhatsApp from the person's name
Take threats to the police
lessons.try_it: Find the Block and Report buttons in WhatsApp without using them.

lessons.title: Getting help and supporting others
lessons.body:
Nobody should deal with bullying, harassment or threats alone.

## Who can help
- **A trusted person:** a family member, friend, teacher, pastor or community leader.
- **School:** teachers and guidance staff must take bullying between pupils seriously, even when it happens on phones.
- **Your workplace:** report harassment by colleagues to a manager or human resources.
- **The police:** for threats, blackmail, sharing intimate images, and harassment that will not stop. Bring your screenshots.
- **Child protection services:** if a child is at risk, organisations such as **Childline Zambia** and the police **Victim Support Unit** help children and families.

## Helping someone who tells you
- **Listen** without blaming them. Do not say *"Why did you send that photo?"*
- Thank them for telling you.
- Help them save evidence and block the person.
- Ask what they would like to do, and offer to go with them to report it.
- Check on them again in the following days.

## Look after your wellbeing
Being attacked online is stressful. It is okay to take a break from social media, mute groups, and spend time with people who support you. If you feel very low, talk to someone you trust or a health worker.

## Remember
Asking for help is a sign of strength. Most problems are easier to solve when they are reported early.
key_points: You do not have to deal with it alone
Listen without blaming
Bring screenshots when you report
lessons.try_it: Save the number of one person you would call if someone threatened you online.

modules.title: Wellbeing and children
modules.summary: Keeping children safe, screen time and your digital footprint.

lessons.title: Helping children stay safe online
lessons.body:
Children are growing up with phones. They learn, play and talk to friends online. They also face risks they may not understand. Your guidance matters more than any setting.

## Talk early and often
- Ask what apps and games they use, and who they talk to. Show interest, not anger.
- Agree simple rules together: which apps, how long, and when phones are put away.
- Tell them they can **always come to you** if something online makes them uncomfortable, and that they will not be punished for telling you.

## Teach the key rules
- Do not share your full name, school, home address or phone number with people you meet online.
- Do not send photos to people you do not know in real life.
- Never agree to meet someone from the internet without a parent.
- Keep passwords private, even from friends.
- If anyone asks you to keep a secret from your parents, tell a parent.

## Warning signs
Be alert if a child becomes secretive about their phone, receives gifts or airtime from unknown people, has a new "friend" who is much older, or seems upset after being online. Adults with bad intentions often start by being very kind and asking for secrecy.

## Useful settings
- **Google Family Link** lets parents manage apps and screen time on a child's Android phone.
- **YouTube Kids** is safer for young children than normal YouTube.
- Set the Play Store to require approval before installing apps.

## If something happens
Stay calm, save evidence, and report to the platform and the police. Childline Zambia and the police Victim Support Unit can help.
key_points: Talk early and keep the door open
Teach: no personal details, no photos, no meeting strangers
Secrecy and gifts from strangers are warning signs
lessons.try_it: Have a short conversation with a child in your life about who they talk to online.

lessons.title: Balancing screen time
lessons.body:
Phones are useful, but they are designed to keep us scrolling. Too much time on screens can affect sleep, work, family time and mood.

## Signs it may be too much
- You pick up your phone without thinking, many times an hour.
- You stay up late scrolling and feel tired the next day.
- You feel worse about yourself after looking at other people's posts.
- Family or friends complain you are always on your phone.

## Check your time
On Android, open **Settings**, then **Digital Wellbeing and parental controls**. It shows how long you spend in each app every day. The number often surprises people.

## Small changes that help
- **Turn off notifications** for apps that are not important. Each buzz pulls you back.
- **Mute busy groups.**
- Use **Bedtime mode** to turn the screen grey at night and silence the phone.
- Keep the phone **out of the bedroom** or face down during meals.
- Set **app timers** in Digital Wellbeing for apps you overuse.
- Replace some scrolling with a walk, a chat with family or a book.

## Remember what is real
Social media shows the best moments of people's lives, often edited. It is not the whole truth. Comparing your everyday life with others' highlights can make you feel bad for no reason.

## Be a good example
Children copy what adults do. Putting your own phone away at meals teaches more than any rule.
key_points: Check your screen time in Digital Wellbeing
Turn off unneeded notifications
Keep phones away at meals and bedtime
lessons.try_it: Open Digital Wellbeing and find which app you used most yesterday.

lessons.title: Your digital footprint
lessons.body:
Everything you do online leaves a trace: posts, comments, photos, likes and even searches. Together these make your **digital footprint**.

## It lasts
Even if you delete a post, someone may already have taken a screenshot or shared it. Things posted years ago can come back.

## Who might look
- **Employers** often search candidates' names before hiring.
- **Schools and scholarship committees.**
- **Customers** deciding whether to trust your business.
- **Criminals** looking for information to trick or rob you.

## Check your own footprint
Search your full name on Google and look at what appears. Check the Images tab too. Then open your Facebook profile and view it as the public sees it: on your profile, tap the three dots and **View as**.

## Clean it up
- Delete or hide old posts you would not want an employer to see.
- Set future posts to **Friends** rather than Public.
- Remove tags from photos you do not like.
- Close old accounts you no longer use.

## Build a good footprint
Your footprint can also help you. Sharing your work, skills, volunteering and helpful posts can show employers and customers who you are. A tidy LinkedIn or business page is a positive footprint.

## Before you post
Ask: *Would I be happy for this to be seen in five years, by a future employer, or by my children?*
key_points: Everything online leaves a lasting trace
Search your name to see your footprint
Share things that show your skills and values
lessons.try_it: Search your full name on Google and look at what appears.
